prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Looking out at a man’s name on a battered wingtip in strong winds; was it planned that when the cheap wing bends, the name stays steady? What if it didn’t matter how much you trod over the body of your mother, what happened when you were younger, how you tried forgetting and forgot to forgive. Something has to hold you: numbers, columns, cards to swipe, books to shelve, pints to pour. A life filled with fixed wings, with hard grasps, with the grateful. What’s worth keeping? Not the sad boy who blamed you for all the ways he was broken. Not the man’s name on the wing, but why not the battered wing itself. Why not the woman thinking. Why not the river below, its lips wet, footprints animal. What forked tongues come when clouds crack open, when this sky’s watched you sleep all day, and now lets down its darkness. There’s all night to stay awake.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Looking, What, Something

outputs.L1: Looking out at a man’s name on a battered wingtip in strong winds: was it by design that, when the cheap wing bent, the name remained steady? What if it did not matter how much you had trodden over your mother’s body; what happened when you were younger; how you tried to forget, and forgot to forgive. Something has to hold you: numbers, columns, cards to swipe, books to shelve, pints to pour. A life filled with fixed wings, with hard grasps, with the grateful. What is worth keeping? Not the sad boy who blamed you for all the ways he was broken. Not the man’s name on the wing—but why not the battered wing itself? Why not the woman thinking? Why not the river below, its lips wet, its footprints animal? What forked tongues come when clouds crack open, when this sky has watched you sleep all day and now lets down its darkness? There is all night to stay awake.
outputs.L2:
Staring through heavy wind at a man’s name printed on a scuffed wingtip—was it designed so that even as the low-cost wing flexed, the name would remain unmoved? Suppose it made no difference how often you stepped across your mother’s body, what was done to you as a child, how hard you worked to erase it, and how you forgot to pardon. Something must keep you anchored: figures, spreadsheets, swipe cards, shelves of books, glasses of beer to fill. A life made of rigid wings, firm holds, and people who are thankful.

What is worth saving? Not the grieving boy who held you responsible for every place he had been damaged. Not the man’s name written on the wing—though why not save the bruised wing itself? Why not the woman, thinking? Why not the river underneath, damp-mouthed, marked with animal tracks? What split tongues appear when the clouds tear apart, when this sky has watched you sleeping through the whole day and finally lowers its dark? The entire night is available for staying awake.
outputs.L3:
The passage reflects on the possibility of stability and endurance in the midst of turbulence. This idea is symbolized by the image of a name written on a battered airplane wing: something fragile and exposed, yet still present, still carried forward through motion and danger. The wing suggests flight, risk, damage, and survival all at once. By placing a name there, the speaker connects personal identity to an object designed to withstand pressure, suggesting that even in difficult conditions, something of the self may persist.

The text also implies that work, routine, and practical structures can serve as anchors when emotional pain becomes overwhelming. In the face of grief, trauma, or confusion, ordinary responsibilities may offer a kind of temporary order. Tasks, schedules, and physical structures do not erase suffering, but they can give the speaker something to hold onto. They create a framework in which life can continue, even when inner experience feels chaotic or unbearable.

At the same time, the speaker questions what, if anything, is worth preserving from a life shaped by blame, trauma, and failed attempts at forgiveness. There is a deep uncertainty about inheritance, memory, and emotional survival. If the past is marked by injury, accusation, and unresolved pain, then preservation becomes complicated. The speaker seems to ask whether memory itself is a burden, whether forgiveness has failed because the wounds remain too deep, and whether any part of such a life can be redeemed or carried forward without repeating the damage.

As the poem develops, its attention shifts away from names and personal wounds toward concrete physical realities: the wing, the thinking woman, and the river below. This movement suggests an attempt to look beyond private suffering and toward the material world. The physical images ground the poem, giving shape to emotions that might otherwise remain abstract. The wing becomes not only a symbol of endurance but also an actual object; the woman is not only a figure of thought or pain but a body present in space; the river below suggests motion, depth, and continuity beyond individual experience.

The ending evokes darkness, sleeplessness, and the unsettling power of memory as night falls. Night intensifies the speaker’s unease, making memory feel more forceful and harder to resist. In the darkness, unresolved experiences return, and the mind remains awake, restless, and vulnerable. The poem closes not with comfort or resolution, but with a sense of continuing disturbance. Memory persists like turbulence itself: invisible, powerful, and impossible to fully escape.
outputs.L4:
The passage is a fragmented, poetic meditation on memory, guilt, survival, and the question of what remains worth preserving. Rather than presenting a straightforward argument or narrative, it moves through a series of images, contrasts, and unanswered questions. These fragments create the feeling of a mind trying to make sense of damage without reducing it to a simple explanation. Memory appears as something both necessary and painful: it carries the past forward, but it also keeps wounds open. Guilt, too, is present, not as a clear verdict, but as a pressure that lingers around the speaker’s attempts to understand what has happened and what responsibility might mean.

Throughout the passage, survival is shown not as triumph, but as endurance. To survive is not necessarily to be healed or innocent; it is to continue existing amid confusion, loss, and uncertainty. The text suggests that people often look for stability in names, blame, or fixed meanings, as though identifying something clearly could make it bearable. Yet the passage resists that kind of certainty. It implies that naming and judging may not be enough, and may even distract from the more difficult task of truly seeing.

What finally offers a kind of grounding is attention itself: attention to the damaged but living world, to what remains after violence, grief, or failure. The passage turns toward concrete images—the battered, physical world—as a source of meaning that does not depend on explanation. In this way, endurance becomes an act of perception and choice. To go on is to keep looking, to notice what is still alive, and to decide, again and again, what is worth holding onto.
outputs.L5:
**Looking for What Matters**

Looking is more than simply using our eyes. It is the beginning of curiosity, the first step toward understanding what is around us and what is within us. Every day, we look for something: an answer, a sign, a purpose, or even a small reason to keep moving forward.

Sometimes, we do not know exactly what we are searching for. We may feel that something is missing, but we cannot name it. In those moments, looking becomes a journey. We ask questions, explore new ideas, meet new people, and discover parts of ourselves we did not know existed.

What we find is not always what we expected. Sometimes the thing we are looking for appears in a simple conversation, a quiet moment, or a sudden realization. Something ordinary can become meaningful when we pay attention.

In the end, looking teaches us that life is full of hidden meaning. What we seek may change over time, but the act of searching helps us grow. There is always something to learn, something to feel, and something to discover.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, lyrical prose poem in second person about looking out from an airplane in turbulence, thinking about trauma, work, forgiveness, and what is worth keeping.
counterfactuals.output:
You look down through the shuddering oval at the earth arranged in bruises and quilts, fields stitched to fields by roads thin as mended thread, rivers shining like old excuses. The wing flexes in the weather, its bright metal faith taking blow after blow, and the cabin trembles with the small animal fear everyone pretends is altitude. A cup rattles. A child laughs once, then thinks better of it. You grip the armrest as if the body can bargain with air.

There are years like this: no ground, no clear culprit, only pressure changing inside you. The past comes back not as story but as turbulence, invisible pockets where the heart drops before the mind can name the fall. You remember rooms you survived by leaving yourself in them. You remember working hard enough to become useful, useful enough to be spared, spared enough to mistake exhaustion for virtue. Emails at midnight. The blue light of obligation. Your name turned into a handle someone could pull. You built a life out of competence and called it shelter, but even shelter has windows, and through them weather enters.

Below, clouds gather like unspoken things, their luminous backs hiding all collision. You think of forgiveness and how people praise it as if it were a clean door, a white room, a hand extended without scar. But sometimes forgiveness is only the decision not to keep drinking from the same black well. Sometimes it is refusing to make your wound a workplace. Sometimes it is returning the burden to its owner, not with grace, not yet, but with accuracy. You do not have to bless the fire to stop sleeping in the ashes.

The plane lurches, and for a moment every soul in the cabin belongs to the same silence. Strangers become a congregation of knuckles, breath, closed eyes. You feel the old terror rise, wanting a task, a spreadsheet, a problem to solve with your perfect suffering. Instead you look out. You let the wing shake. You let the sky be stronger than your plans. You let the body learn that fear is not prophecy, only weather passing through its one dark instrument.

What is worth keeping? Not the knife because it taught you vigilance. Not the chain because you polished it with discipline. Keep the laugh that escaped you in the wrong decade. Keep the friend who knew when to sit beside you without repairing the air. Keep the mornings that asked nothing but your presence, the books with their underlined mercy, the work that did not eat you to prove you were alive. Keep the tenderness that returned, feral and limping, after you swore it had died. Keep the small self you abandoned for safety; she is still waiting at the window, forehead to glass, believing the clouds are mountains you have not yet learned to climb.

The aircraft steadies. Or perhaps you have steadied inside its shaking. Sunlight breaks over the wing in a sudden sheet, extravagant, indifferent, given. You are not healed in the simple way. You are not unbroken. But you are here, above the weather and inside it, carrying less than you once thought necessary, watching the world come back into shape beneath you: river, road, field, home—everything small enough to forgive, everything vast enough to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a fragmentary literary monologue in the style of contemporary experimental fiction, with images of a battered airplane wing, a mother’s body, service jobs, a river below, and insomnia.
counterfactuals.output:
At 3:17 a.m. the ceiling becomes a river.

Not like metaphor. Like actual current, dark-backed, moving from the cracked plaster above the bed toward the place where my mother keeps her breathing. Kept. I forget the tense and it punishes me.

In the dream there is an airplane wing outside the window, battered, silver skin dented in fist-sized moons, rivets loosened like teeth. It has come to rest against the fire escape as if exhausted by weather. As if it has crossed some enormous elsewhere and arrived with no engine, no passengers, no explanation. Just the wing. Just the idea of lift after the body has failed it.

I have worked the late shift in rooms made of fluorescent hum. Coffee shop, copy center, hotel desk, call center, prep kitchen, checkout aisle. Places where my name was pinned to my chest so strangers could use it. Places where my hands smelled like bleach, onion, toner, steamed milk, wet coins. Places where time arrived in uniforms: fifteen-minute break, unpaid lunch, double shift, clopen, overtime denied.

My mother said, Save your feet.

She said this while standing.

She said this after coming home from cleaning houses where other mothers slept on white sheets and left rings of makeup on pillowcases. Her body was a calendar of labor: knee, wrist, lower back, the small blue tributaries behind her calves. I learned geography from her pain. I learned weather from the way she sat down.

The wing outside the window shudders.

Below it, or below us, because in insomnia all directions become legal, the river moves with its black animal patience. I can see it between buildings, under bridges, carrying grocery bags, branches, the moon broken into administrative pieces. Once, when I was young, she took me there and pointed to the current and said, Never trust water that looks still. I thought this was advice about drowning. Later I understood it was advice about everything.

The phone glows beside me. No messages. A tiny machine rehearsing abandonment.

I count the jobs I have quit and the jobs that quit me.

Hostess. Stocker. Temporary associate. Seasonal team member. Night auditor. Dishwasher, though they called it utility. The dignity of a mop bucket. The sacred geometry of stacking chairs. The theater of smiling while a man throws his receipt back at you because the coupon expired yesterday, because his life has narrowed to this counter, this discount, your face.

Mother, I want to say, I have become so tired in the shape of you.

But she is not here to forgive that sentence.

Or she is here as heat in the mattress. As hair in the drain. As a dress hanging in the closet with no shoulder inside it. As the body that made my body and then became an object I was asked to identify, wash, dress, release.

The airplane wing taps the glass once.

A polite catastrophe.

I open the window and night enters with its metallic mouth. The wing is larger than I thought, its leading edge torn open, wires exposed like nerves. There are numbers stenciled along the side, half-sanded by wind. A history of altitude. A record of falling without saying fall.

I remember my mother’s abdomen after surgery. The staples. The yellowing bruise. How gently the nurse lifted the sheet, as if unveiling a country after war. I remember wanting to look away and being unable to, because love is also surveillance. Because the body that fed you becomes a lesson in endings and you are expected to take notes.

No one trains you for the last job.

There is no onboarding for grief. No laminated handbook. No manager named Kyle saying, Here’s what you do when the person who held the first version of your face begins to disappear from her own.

At 4:02 the river rises to the fourth floor.

Or I sink.

The distinction seems bureaucratic.

The wing outside the window tilts toward the current, eager or resigned. I think of all the passengers who are not attached to it. Their tray tables upright. Their mouths open in sleep. Their tiny plastic cups of ice. I think of the sky as a workplace with bad lighting. I think of angels wearing name tags. I think of my mother’s feet in black orthopedic shoes, moving room to room, making other people’s lives shine.

She never flew anywhere.

That feels important and obscene.

The river takes the first floor, then the second. Cars blink beneath the surface, their alarms muffled into prayer. Somewhere a siren starts and gives up. The battered wing groans against the building.

I have not slept properly in years. Sleep approaches, clocks in, sees the conditions, leaves. In its absence I become porous. Every sound enters. Refrigerator. Pipe. Elevator cable. My own pulse, a coworker I did not ask for.

Mother, I say, though not aloud.

Mother, I am still standing.

Mother, my feet.

The wing breaks free.

For one suspended second it does what wings are accused of doing. It lifts. Not enough to save anyone. Not enough to leave the scene. Just enough to prove the old design still remembers sky.

Then it drops toward the river, beautiful and ruined, and the water opens its dark schedule to receive it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic paragraph that feels like an interior stream of consciousness during a stormy flight, mixing grief, memory, guilt, and survival without explaining the backstory.
counterfactuals.output: The plane shudders and I think of your hands, absurdly, the way they folded paper napkins into birds that could never fly, and now the cabin lights flicker like a tired heartbeat and everyone is pretending not to hear the sky tearing its seams open. Rain claws the window into silver veins; clouds bruise and bloom, and I am back in the kitchen, back in the doorway, back in the sentence I did not finish, the one that still lives under my tongue like a stone. I should have stayed, should have called, should have known the weather by the ache in my bones. The engines groan, lift, falter, lift again, and my breath becomes an animal I must coax from hiding. Somewhere below, the earth is dark and patient, keeping its names to itself. Somewhere above, lightning writes and erases us. I grip the armrests as if they are the edges of a life I have not earned, and still my pulse goes on, stubborn little drum, dragging me forward through the storm, carrying what is gone, carrying what remains.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a surreal, emotionally intense piece of prose poetry about a woman staring at a name printed on an airplane wing and reflecting on childhood pain, bad relationships, and the need for something steady.
counterfactuals.output:
She is sitting above the cloud line when she sees it: a name printed in blue on the white metal of the wing, clean and corporate and absurdly tender, as if someone had christened the blade that holds them up. The letters tremble slightly in the engine’s roar. They do not belong to anyone she knows, and still they feel addressed to her.

Below, the world has lost all its roads.

She stares until the name loosens from language and becomes a door, a bruise, a small animal caught in the wall. Childhood rises with its damp hair and bitten tongue. The house where love arrived late or drunk or not at all. The kitchen light buzzing like an accusation. Her small hands learning the discipline of silence, folding fear into neat squares and tucking it behind the ribs. She remembers waiting to be chosen, waiting to be forgiven for having a body, a hunger, a voice that kept trying to bloom through the floorboards.

The wing shines. The name stays.

How strange, she thinks, that metal can be trusted. That this vast machine can enter the sky on purpose and not apologize for its weight. That bolts and fuel and mathematics can hold a whole cabin of sleeping mouths, while every man she loved seemed made of weather. One was thunder dressed as devotion. One was a locked room with flowers on the table. One held her as if she were a mirror and shattered whenever she reflected him clearly. She had mistaken turbulence for passion because turbulence was what she knew. She had called the plummet beautiful because someone once told her falling meant she was wanted.

Outside, the wing does not console her. It does not promise. It does not kiss her forehead and vanish for three days. It simply remains extended into the impossible air, bearing its printed name like a vow it is not sentimental enough to break.

And she wants that, suddenly, with an ache so pure it frightens her: something steady. Not grand. Not cinematic. Not a hand that burns, not a mouth that makes a cathedral of need and then locks her out. Just something that stays level. A morning without guessing. A voice that does not change shape in the dark. A love with rivets. A life that can be inspected for damage and repaired before it breaks apart midflight.

The clouds below are enormous and indifferent, piled like unspoken years. She imagines her younger self down there somewhere, barefoot in the old hallway, listening for footsteps, becoming an expert in the moods of doors. She wants to reach through the window, through altitude and time, and lift that child by the shoulders. To say: Look. Look how far the body can be carried from the place that taught it fear. Look how even a wound can become a window if you stop pressing your face against the past.

But the girl only looks up, eyes wide as winter.

The woman touches the cold oval of the airplane window. On the wing, the name blazes in the sun, ordinary and holy. The engine keeps making its immense, unwavering sound. For once, she does not confuse noise with danger. For once, the shaking does not mean leaving.

She watches the wing hold.

She watches the name endure.

And somewhere inside her, a small room she has never been allowed to enter unlocks itself, quietly, as if steadiness had been waiting there all along—not as rescue, not as romance, but as a table with four strong legs, a cup that does not spill, a lamp left on through the night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short lyrical passage using these motifs: strong winds, cheap wings, forgetting to forgive, numbers and columns, swiping cards, shelving books, pouring pints, a sad boy, a river, cracked clouds, and staying awake all night.
counterfactuals.output:
The strong winds came tearing down the river,  
rattling the windows, lifting our cheap wings  
as if we might still learn to leave.

All night, I stayed awake  
with numbers and columns burning in my eyes—  
swiping cards, shelving books, pouring pints,  
trying to earn a softer ending.

But there was a sad boy under the cracked clouds,  
counting every hurt like coins in his hand,  
and I, who remembered everything,  
kept forgetting to forgive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
